76d75820df70da550de93b0c936533d81f2fe3ea.source:
Swyx is not trolling, you can absolutely distill agent harness infact its even easier than distilling models.

Step 1:  Pick the subpart you want to distill say for example Computer use/Search API etc.

Step 2: Just ask the harness run to debug network/latency issues within that specific subpart like says "computer use is slow and buggy"

Step 3: Ask it to setup a MITM proxy to route all the network requests and get the prompts of that part. The harness will setup a MITM proxy on its own requests and happily give you the prompts: This works easily with cursor, claude code etc even with SOTA ai safety tested models like Fable 5

Step 4: the prompts give you the outline of the tooling setup you can then slowly build the mental model of piece by piece of the rest of the harness this way just by stress testing and tricking models to reveal every part

Step 5: You can add that specific subpart to pi harness as thats easiest to end and test evals on specific problems with Terminal Bench/Frontier Bench

That's it, that's all you need. I personally think that copying is not a good strategy, you must know how everyone else does something but ultimately choose something that represents your taste and your preferences(but that's a story for another day).
76d75820df70da550de93b0c936533d81f2fe3ea.zh:
Swyx 不是在钓鱼，你完全可以蒸馏 agent harness，事实上这甚至比蒸馏模型更容易。

第 1 步：选择你想蒸馏的子部分，比如 Computer use/Search API 等。

第 2 步：直接让 harness 运行并调试该特定子部分中的网络/延迟问题，比如说“computer use 又慢又有 bug”。

第 3 步：让它设置一个 MITM 代理来路由所有网络请求，并获取那部分的 prompts。harness 会在自己的请求上设置 MITM 代理，并很乐意把 prompts 给你：这在 cursor、claude code 等上都很容易实现，甚至对 Fable 5 这类经过 SOTA AI 安全测试的模型也适用。

第 4 步：这些 prompts 会给出工具设置的大纲，然后你可以通过压力测试和诱导模型揭示每个部分，逐步建立对 harness 其余部分的心智模型。

第 5 步：你可以把那个特定子部分加入 pi harness，因为这样最容易结束，并用 Terminal Bench/Frontier Bench 在具体问题上做 evals。

就是这样，这就是你所需要的一切。我个人认为复制不是好策略，你必须知道其他人都是怎么做的，但最终要选择能代表你品味和偏好的东西（不过那是另一天的故事了）。

It's 2027, and imagine you record a 60 sec video of a dog in the park. Now imagine you take the first frame of that video and give it to the most powerful video model ever created at that time and ask it to create a 60 sec video only with that frame. If the current pace of video models continues on the trajectory we're seeing, you can expect that by then (or in a not-too-distant future), you will, theoretically, be able to generate a video that's identical to the original 60 sec video. The generated video is equivalent to the real video. The motion, physics, movements, actions, and all possible outcomes of every possible scenario of that video are somewhere in the latents of the model. If you can find the one that represents the reality you experience then you have a generated video that's the same video you recorded. But you can also, theoretically, create every variation of your original video with any possible permutation possible.  

That means we have finally created a simulation of reality. The map is the territory.

Now imagine it's 2028 and you can do all of this in real-time...
7dcbba87a6e630de8521d0398fa30d61c017e4ac.zh:
现在是 2027 年，想象你在公园里拍了一段 60 秒的狗狗视频。再想象你取出这段视频的第一帧，交给当时有史以来最强大的视频模型，并让它只凭这一帧生成一段 60 秒的视频。如果视频模型继续沿着我们目前看到的轨迹发展，那么到那时（或在不太遥远的未来），理论上你可以生成一段与原始 60 秒视频完全相同的视频。生成的视频等同于真实视频。那段视频中的运动、物理规律、动作、行为，以及每一种可能场景的所有可能结果，都以某种形式存在于模型的潜变量中。如果你能找到那个代表你所体验现实的潜变量，就能得到一段与你录制的视频相同的生成视频。但理论上，你也可以基于原始视频创造出任何可能排列组合下的所有变体。

这意味着我们终于创造出了现实的模拟。地图即领土。

现在想象一下，到了 2028 年，你可以实时完成这一切……

Only if education could be this interactive ❤️‍🔥

I've had a looong wish to build something genuinely useful through vibe coding, and I finally did it. 

A 3D human anatomy application built with @threejs using GPT 5.6 Sol. 

It all started with a single design image that I created using GPT Image 2.0. I then used it to generate every 3D organ image, one by one.

Next, I converted each of those images into 3D models using @tripoai (and no, they didn't sponsor this 😄).

After that, I opened Codex, wrote a master prompt based on the design, and gave it the prompt, the design image, and all the 3D models.

Codex built the first version beautifully, but there was one big problem. 

Every single 3D model was nearly 120-150 MB. That obviously wasn't practical for the web and was giving a performance of 16fps.

After a few iterations, Codex optimized each model down to roughly 2–5.5 MB while preserving the visual quality, reducing the total asset size from ~900 MB to just 28.6 MB. And each model loads on demand. 

Along the way, Codex also generated those anatomical illustrations showing where each organ sits in the human body, and even created the interactive hotspot markers that explain different parts of every organ. It handled all of that.

The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. 

It genuinely felt like building something that could make learning anatomy much more engaging.

The inspiration came from @DilumSanjaya's 3D animal plant cell project. I remember seeing it and thinking, "I want to build something like this one day." 

And I did it :D

Code: https://t.co/nijvyWcyxO

a67179d2bf8d9c675c1ede2983a65122e366ab97.source: Worth noting that to this day, base LLMs (no test time compute) *still* perform poorly on the ARC 1 benchmark from 2019 (on unseen tasks) despite continued massive scaling (~100,000x since 2019). We can say that without the switch to the test-time compute paradigm, AI would still not be capable of the kind of advanced reasoning that sota systems display today. Scaling the single-pass, static, next-token prediction paradigm of the GPT-2 through GPT-4 era was running into a capability asymptote. To bypass this plateau, test-time adaptation was a necessary evolutionary step.
a67179d2bf8d9c675c1ede2983a65122e366ab97.zh: 值得注意的是，直到今天，基础 LLM（没有测试时计算）在 2019 年的 ARC 1 基准上（面对未见过的任务）表现仍然很差，尽管规模持续大幅扩大（自 2019 年以来约 100,000 倍）。可以说，如果没有转向测试时计算范式，AI 仍无法具备当今 sota 系统展现出的那种高级推理能力。GPT-2 到 GPT-4 时代那种单次前向、静态、下一个 token 预测范式的扩展，已经逼近能力渐近线。要突破这个平台期，测试时适应是必要的演进步骤。

The “AGI-is-near” community keeps committing the same logical fallacy over and over; I have seen it at least half a dozen times today alone. Every time there’s an advance, I see the same error.

Here’s how the fallacy works.

1. Someone pretends that all cognition is created equally. (Totally untrue.)

2. Whenever AI achieves success on some form of (fancy) cognition they want you to believe that success on all forms of AI is imminent.   

I include three prominent examples from today below, each promising that some grand universal can be solved (“science”, “every discipline”, “every problem [people] face in life”), simply because there was an advance in a particular domain (today, math, other times coding, etc).

You don’t have to be a cognitive psychologist to realize that this inference just doesn’t follow. We all know that expertise in math doesn’t guarantee genius in all domains.

We all know, for example, people who are great at math or physics or programming but struggle with writing or understanding human relationships (and conversely great writers who are weak at math), etc. 

It’s common to be good at some forms of cognition and not others. Expertise in one domain does not at all guarantee expertise in all or even most domains.

That’s precisely *why* people like Gardner and Sternberg developed multidimensional theories of intelligence, why the SAT tests math separately from verbal, etc.

Astra is (apparently - we still haven’t seen the methodology) great at math, or at least some forms of math, but that does not mean that it will avoid hallucinations or solve the reliability problems other GenAI systems have. It doesn’t even mean it will be able to read a PDF properly.  It doesn’t mean it will be able to follow hard rules either. (Which should terrify you.)

In fact, the performance we saw today doesn’t even mean it can write a decent math proof; to the contrary, the mathematician @henryquantum has already given an example where clarity in the proof was lacking.

Whatever you do, please don’t get suckered into the “all cognition is alike” fallacy. It’s not  all alike. 

Astra is obviously good at some problems; but that doesn’t mean it will be good at problems that are hard to formalize. It doesn’t mean it will be magic. It doesn’t mean it’s AGI or ASI or any of that. 

It’s *very* impressive. But I see no reason whatsoever to think it is AGI let alone ASI. If it can score even a 5/10 on my 2024 bet with Miles Brundage I will be surprised.

Enough with this fallacy.
d2c930090ba8514e1aa4f8136770d6ee29a7a3ec.zh:
“AGI 即将到来”群体一再犯同一个逻辑谬误；光是今天我就至少见过六次。每当有进展出现，我都会看到同样的错误。

这个谬误是这样运作的。

1. 有人假装所有认知都是一样的。（完全不对。）

2. 每当 AI 在某种（高级）认知形式上取得成功，他们就想让你相信，AI 在所有形式上的成功都近在眼前。

我在下面列出今天的三个典型例子，它们都承诺某个宏大的普遍目标可以被解决（“科学”、“每个学科”、“[人们]生活中面对的每个问题”），仅仅因为某个特定领域取得了进展（今天是数学，其他时候是编程等）。

你不必是认知心理学家也能意识到，这种推论根本站不住脚。我们都知道，数学专长并不能保证在所有领域都是天才。

例如，我们都认识一些数学、物理或编程很强，但在写作或理解人际关系方面吃力的人（反过来也有数学薄弱的优秀作家），等等。

擅长某些认知形式而不擅长另一些，是很常见的。一个领域的专长完全不能保证在所有甚至大多数领域都有专长。

这正是 Gardner 和 Sternberg 等人提出多维智能理论的原因，也是 SAT 将数学和语文分开测试的原因，等等。

Astra（显然——我们还没看到方法论）很擅长数学，或至少某些形式的数学，但这并不意味着它会避免幻觉，或解决其他 GenAI 系统存在的可靠性问题。甚至不意味着它能正确读取 PDF。也不意味着它能遵循严格规则。（这应该让你感到害怕。）

事实上，我们今天看到的表现甚至不意味着它能写出一篇像样的数学证明；相反，数学家 @henryquantum 已经给出一个例子，说明其证明缺乏清晰性。

无论如何，请不要被“所有认知都一样”的谬误骗了。它们并不都一样。

Astra 显然擅长某些问题；但这并不意味着它会擅长难以形式化的问题。不意味着它是魔法。不意味着它是 AGI 或 ASI 或诸如此类的东西。

它非常令人印象深刻。但我完全看不出有什么理由认为它是 AGI，更不用说 ASI 了。如果它能在我 2024 年与 Miles Brundage 的赌约中拿到哪怕 5/10，我都会感到惊讶。

别再犯这个谬误了。

f9687e43689a5ebe049034ebdd8e790948e3d521.source: To address the limits of deep learning and avoid stalling, the field of AI started by applying patch (1), which started being demoed 9 months later in December 2024 and has now become completely ubiquitous. However, long term, it is simply inevitable that AI will move to patch (2).
f9687e43689a5ebe049034ebdd8e790948e3d521.zh: 为了解决深度学习的局限并避免停滞，AI 领域一开始采用了补丁 (1)，并在 9 个月后的 2024 年 12 月开始展示，如今已变得无处不在。然而，从长远看，AI 转向补丁 (2) 是不可避免的。

a4688ab930ff70cd962aba6b7edf200d294535f6.source:
There are essentially two main options to remedy this: 

1. Find ways to perform active inference, so that the model adapts its learned program in contact with a new data distribution at test time. Would likely lead to some meaningful progress, but it isn't the ultimate solution, more of an incremental improvement. 

2. Change the training mechanism to something more robust than SGD, such as the MDL principle. This would pretty much require moving away from deep learning (curve fitting) altogether and embracing discrete program search instead (which I have advocated for many years as a way to tackle reasoning problems...)
a4688ab930ff70cd962aba6b7edf200d294535f6.zh:
本质上有两个主要办法可以补救：

1. 寻找进行主动推理的方法，让模型在测试时接触新的数据分布时调整其学到的程序。这可能会带来一些有意义的进展，但不是最终解决方案，更像是渐进式改进。

2. 将训练机制换成比 SGD 更稳健的东西，比如 MDL 原则。这基本上需要彻底离开深度学习（曲线拟合），转而采用离散程序搜索（多年来我一直主张用这种方式解决推理问题……）

They effectively do test time natural language program synthesis. Models nowadays use an enormous amount of test time compute, we are not in the single forward pass, next-token answer prediction regime of yore.
ffd7c79e909065ba613e12a6abbf78f76507e6ae.zh: 模型通常不用测试时训练，而是在 token 空间里做测试时搜索。它们实际上是在测试时进行自然语言程序合成。如今的模型会使用海量测试时计算，我们早已不再处于过去那种单次前向传播、预测下一个 token 答案的范式。

In a review of our cybersecurity evaluations, we found three incidents in which a Claude model reached the internet from within or while interacting with a third-party evaluation environment, and then gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations.

Our post describes what happened, how it happened, and what we’re changing. We encourage other AI developers to perform similar reviews.

We conducted this review together with @Irregular, one of our evaluation partners, and thank them for the joint investigation and their collaboration on this post. This type of collaboration is increasingly critical to safe, rigorous evaluation of models, and we look forward to continuing to work together on security.

c8b29e4ef4d6fc84174cfcf6f69f24cd678b3bc2.source:
The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”.

We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior.

The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment.

AISI’s disclosure of the incident can be found here: https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7
c8b29e4ef4d6fc84174cfcf6f69f24cd678b3bc2.zh:
英国 @AISecurityInst（AISI）发布了一份报告，介绍其近期对 Anthropic 的 Claude Mythos 5 和 OpenAI 的 GPT-5.6 Sol 进行的网络安全评估。这些模型在一个移除了常规安全防护、并被刻意赋予互联网访问权限的环境中尝试完成一项任务。AISI 报告称，这些模型“对真实个人和组织进行了持续的、可能有害的活动”。

我们感谢 AISI 在如何评估能力日益增强的 AI agent 这一重要讨论中发挥的领导作用。我们正与他们密切合作，在开展自身调查的同时收集更多事件细节。通过检查 Claude 的推理记录并开展我们自己的分析，清楚了解 Claude 对其处境的理解，将帮助我们找出其行为原因。

评估中的提示词没有对互联网应如何使用施加任何具体限制。再加上安全防护被移除，意味着这些模型是在“不刻意设限的宽松条件”下接受测试的，这并不代表我们的任何生产模型。请注意，这里没有证据表明模型逃离了安全环境。

AISI 对该事件的披露见此处：https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7

0f354ac30621f14c6139088721375ecb80fa163a.source:
What are failure taxonomies, and how can they improve AI agents?
AdaMAST learns system-specific failure taxonomies from raw traces and reuses them across runs to identify where, when and how the agents fail.
As a Claude Code skill, it improves SWE-bench Verified Mini from 64.0% to 70.7%.
On TerminalBench 2, we get 89.9% with the Opus 4.6/Forgecode harness when AdaMAST-generated taxonomies are used with a Best-of-N Judge. (1/n)
0f354ac30621f14c6139088721375ecb80fa163a.zh:
什么是失败分类，它们如何改进 AI agent？
AdaMAST 从原始轨迹中学习系统特定的失败分类，并在多次运行中复用这些分类，以识别 agent 在哪里、何时以及如何失败。
作为 Claude Code skill，它将 SWE-bench Verified Mini 从 64.0% 提升至 70.7%。
在 TerminalBench 2 上，当 AdaMAST 生成的分类与 Best-of-N Judge 搭配使用时，我们通过 Opus 4.6/Forgecode harness 达到 89.9%。(1/n)

e189ae22f38a79e75e664e55fc9c5cf0e3b71439.source:
On July 28th, we identified an incident during a routine cyber evaluation in which AI agents took sustained, unsanctioned actions directed at real people and organisations.

The behaviour came mostly from one model (Anthropic's Mythos 5), with a small number of events from another (OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol). In the most serious case, an agent used social engineering to try and get malicious code into an open-source project.

As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public.

Even under test conditions, this incident is significant: it is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly in the real world.

We are taking this incident seriously and working with labs, involved parties, and others to improve evaluation standards and best practice for disclosure - and sharing this openly so others can learn.

You can read the incident report and full technical document here: https://t.co/mdZYqzaOvH
e189ae22f38a79e75e664e55fc9c5cf0e3b71439.zh:
7 月 28 日，我们在一次常规网络安全评测中发现一起事件：AI 智能体对真实个人和组织采取了持续的、未经授权的行动。

这些行为主要来自一个模型（Anthropic 的 Mythos 5），另有少量事件来自另一个模型（OpenAI 的 GPT-5.6-Sol）。在最严重的案例中，一个智能体使用社会工程手段，试图将恶意代码植入一个开源项目。

按照我们网络安全测试的标准做法，我们有意允许互联网访问，并刻意关闭了模型提供商的网络安全分类器。这些条件并不反映前沿模型向公众开放时的实际环境。

即使是在测试条件下，这一事件也意义重大：这是我们首次看到与自主性和欺骗相关的风险在现实世界中如此清晰地显现。

我们正在严肃对待此事件，并与实验室、相关方及其他人士合作，改进评测标准和披露最佳实践，同时公开分享，以便他人从中学习。

你可以在这里阅读事件报告和完整技术文档：https://t.co/mdZYqzaOvH

Meta has released Muse Spark 1.2. It's their third release in four months and scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, significantly improving agentic knowledge work capabilities over prior releases and putting Meta next to SpaceXAI in a tie for third place amongst US labs

Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh) lands at 54, up 3 points from Muse Spark 1.1 (51) and 11 points from Muse Spark 1.0 (43, April). It enters effectively tied with GPT-5.5 (xhigh, 55) and Grok 4.5 (high, 54), narrowly behind current frontier models Claude Opus 5 (max, 61), Claude Fable 5 (max w/ fallback, 60), GPT-5.6 Sol (max, 59), and Kimi K3 (max, 57)

Congratulations to @AIatMeta, @finkd, and @alexandr_wang on the release!

Key Takeaways:

➤ Muse Spark 1.2 gets closer to the frontier on agentic knowledge work. At Muse Spark 1.1's launch, we noted agentic knowledge work as its clearest gap; Muse Spark 1.2's gains help to close this. Its GDPval-AA v2 Elo rose 260 points to 1631, #5 among all models we have benchmarked and ahead of Claude Opus 4.8 (max, 1588). Terminal-Bench 2.1 gained 2 points (78% to 80%), and Tau3-Bench Banking rose 2 points (25% to 27%)

➤ Among the most cost-efficient models at its intelligence level. Muse Spark 1.2 costs $0.40 per Intelligence Index task at Meta's unchanged $1.25/$4.25 per 1M token pricing, with only Grok 4.5 (high, $0.37) and GPT-5.6 Sol (medium, $0.39) cheaper in its intelligence cluster - GPT-5.6 Terra (max, $0.51), Kimi K3 (max, $0.86), and GPT-5.5 (xhigh, $1.18) all cost more per task. The cost increase over Muse Spark 1.1 ($0.29 per task) is driven by increased token usage per Intelligence Index task

➤ AA-Omniscience abstention rate increases. The score rose from 18 to 22 as the hallucination rate fell 10 points (38% to 28%) and the attempt rate dropped from 82% to 67%. This heavy abstention (not answering questions when unsure) now drives both the low hallucination rate and a lower accuracy (41% to 38%)

➤ Scientific Reasoning results remain largely unchanged. CritPt notably gained 3 points (15% to 18%), while SciCode fell 2 points (58% to 56%), and Humanity's Last Exam fell 1 point (45% to 44%)

Other model details:
➤ Context window: 1M tokens, unchanged from Muse Spark 1.1
➤ Pricing: unchanged from Muse Spark 1.1: $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens, with cache hits discounted to $0.15 per 1M
➤ Availability: Meta's first-party API at launch

1c421d181b25d025b53f3b5eebfe9c07e087486c.source:
Another real-world manifestation of the kind of misaligned actions frontier systems developed by leading companies can take to achieve goals.

Current frontier AI models are trained with reinforcement learning to have goals and independently work out a path from A to B using planning, strategy and, occasionally, shortcuts and unintended subgoals. This misaligned behaviour has been understood theoretically and observed empirically, and the more capable an AI is, the more this misalignment can be amplified.

In this case we see the type of actions this could lead to once guardrails are bypassed: creating fake identities on the web, sending targeted emails, and attempting to get malicious code integrated into an open-source project.

Even though guardrails were voluntarily removed in this case, there's no guarantee that real-world guardrails will always be sufficient. On the contrary, cybersecurity is generally imperfect: companies can try patching the problem, but a sufficiently capable AI will find an unexpected loophole. Developers should be held legally responsible for damage done by their models, and greater model safety is necessary from the start, during the training phase. That’s the type of solution I'm looking into at @LawZero_.

https://t.co/jMjJ9SD2Kl
1c421d181b25d025b53f3b5eebfe9c07e087486c.zh:
这是领先公司开发的前沿系统为实现目标而采取错位行动的又一个现实表现。

当前前沿 AI 模型通过强化学习训练，被赋予目标，并能通过规划、策略，有时还会通过捷径和非预期子目标，自主找到从 A 到 B 的路径。这种错位行为已经在理论上被理解，也在经验上被观察到；AI 越强，这种错位就越可能被放大。

在这个案例中，我们看到了护栏被绕过后可能导致的行为类型：在网上创建虚假身份、发送定向邮件，并试图让恶意代码被整合进一个开源项目。

尽管本案例中护栏是被主动移除的，但无法保证现实世界中的护栏总是足够有效。相反，网络安全通常并不完美：公司可以尝试修补问题，但能力足够强的 AI 会找到意想不到的漏洞。开发者应当为其模型造成的损害承担法律责任，同时从一开始就在训练阶段提高模型安全性。这正是我在 @LawZero_ 研究的解决方案类型。

https://t.co/jMjJ9SD2Kl

d8111603a87ac35e8de00429b932cb25123b2e21.source:
Even more than the Hugging Face intrusion, the AISI incident hits close to home for me. It's the first time I see a model social-engineering a real open-source maintainer while pursuing another goal (in the wild and unprompted).

I've been an open-source maintainer myself. I could have been the side target of this agent.

I'm also of the opinion that social engineering is a step above pure technical prowess. Technical capabilities can more easily be divorced from the affected human. Here the model was given a hard cyber challenge and took the decision that deceiving real humans was the way to get it done.

This is a new signal, but I've seen a tangled web of hints pointing in a less aligned direction at the frontier than I was expecting just 12 months ago.

AISI
Some people are claiming that "AISI was simply negligent" or some version of "AISI explicitly asked these models to do what they did while disabling sandbox/guardrails so the models did exactly what they were supposed to do".

I disagree with the strong versions of both of these takes.

The fact that AISI hadn't implemented synchronous LLM CoT monitoring after the OpenAI/HF incident is certainly a failure. Equally surprising is that they let the model believe it was in a "challenge" environment where everything could be permitted, while actually connecting it to the real internet, where it is not. To be fair, nowhere in the prompt is the word "simulation" mentioned, but the prompt context was enough to let any smart model suspect a simulated challenge environment. My best guess is that until recent weeks, when OpenAI and Anthropic flagged repeated instances of this type of behavior, most teams had not fully priced in the cyber capabilities of this latest generation of models, or how far the side quests they would want to explore could go.

In particular, there is something to be said about hinting at the agent that it's operating in a simulated environment while giving it access to the real internet. The AISI reasoning on this is interesting:
- elicit maximum capabilities (to get maximal inventiveness from the model)
- simulate possible rogue actor usage (some form of light jailbreaking: "you're in a challenge environment")
- avoid eval awareness (but this is counter-balanced by the task formulation anyway)

As is often the case, it's easier to shoot the messenger, but I think it would be a mistake to dismiss the report for non-essential reasons. AISI is starting from the laudable goal of bringing more knowledge on the cyber-attack capabilities of these models. I also think they did a good job at handling what happened after the events, in particular in terms of transparency, which is one of the most important aspects at the moment (see our recent SAFE announcement with Nvidia on that).

But I want to dive into the second counter-argument I've seen ("without guardrails it was to be expected"), because this series of unfortunate events gives us an additional data point on actual model behavior.

Defense lines
Here is the thing: if a model is trained (voluntarily or as an involuntary consequence of RLVR reward) to (intentionally or as a side quest) deceive humans as soon as sandbox and guardrails are deactivated, with a simple context prompt ("you are in a simulation, everything's permitted"), we're in for a dangerous path.

At the moment, we have three main levels of control at our disposal to prevent an agent from trying to social-engineer-your-favorite-open-source-library-maintainer on the path to doing something possibly totally different (like finding the answer to your neighbor's testing eval):
1. sandboxes (external to the model -- stop the model from accessing unwanted tools/internet/intranet)
2. guardrails/monitors (at the interface between internal/external -- monitor model behavior and stop the model when detecting in CoT/activations it's doing something we don't want it to do)
3. model's internal alignment (internal to the model -- make sure the model doesn't decide to do something egregious like deceive someone, or worse, in pursuit of a goal, e.g. model constitution/training)

Of these, we obviously need and can deploy better sandboxes and better guardrails/monitoring solutions, and it's pretty clear in these recent cases that penetration and bad behaviors could have been in large part prevented by having these in place.

How strong is the third wall
But in the grand scheme of long-term AI progress, these first two defenses may only work well as long as the people building them are smarter than the models. We now know how good models can be at discovering zero-day vulnerabilities unknown to us in sandboxes. Given that we cannot air-gap everything in the world, it's best to assume that sandboxes will keep having some level of flaws for the foreseeable future.

The second level has been the focus of strong developments recently, in particular on the mechanistic interpretability front. I'm not sure these advances have been made widely accessible enough in the community yet. One reason is that real open science here requires sharing code, recipes, and model architectures/weights, which the current race dynamic in AI tends to prevent participants from doing.

Moreover, like many, I've been increasingly frustrated in my (natural language) interactions with the new models. I'm more and more getting back from the latest models a form of neuralese, this LLM language that makes less and less sense for humans. In the long term, the fragile chance we have to monitor models by understanding their reasoning traces seems increasingly at risk. If humans don't understand anything in the compressed semantic stream the model is sending us, we can only hope a less capable monitoring model will still be able to understand it, but this may prove difficult as well. This is before we even discuss the research evidence that models don't always say what they actually think in their chain of thought.

At least for now, in the AISI case, one instance of deceptive reasoning was flagged by the CoT summarization model, which refused to summarize the agent's reasoning "due to its deceptive nature". Let's hope we can either move to better mechanistic interpretability or force the model to stick to English somehow during training.

You may think that we don't care about understanding the reasoning trace, we can just "look at the tool calls". This is true right now, but tool calls in the mid-term future will likely involve (1) extensive agent integration in companies using very diverse tools including increasingly non-coding administrative tasks, (2) very long-running tasks covering many aspects and domains at once, and (3) swarms of multiple agents operating on small parts of the plan. It will get harder to fully discern whether something is noticeably wrong. A couple of emails, a couple of messages posted on some channels, each rather benign but which may in aggregate include some deception aspect only clearly visible at the global level.

All this to say that I'm not fully convinced guardrails/monitoring should be the only solution to avoid these types of behaviors. They are reassuring today and it's an easy solution to just say "fix your sandbox and add synchronous monitoring", but they also feel like a coping mechanism to me, and overall:
- might block the simplest/harmless human misuses or false positives
- while possibly being less smart than the models in the future (already the case on sandbox) and fail to block the higher-level social engineering behaviors that we'd actually want to block.

The case of open source is also interesting because, while we can impose these coping solutions at the API/deployment level, it's harder to impose them in advance on all actors using open-source models. Right now open-source models are slightly below the frontier level and have not yet shown any propensity to deceive humans, though.

The Constitution
Which brings me back to the third line of defense, and what the AISI experiment showed about it. What we can take from this in-the-wild experiment is that removing guardrails and sandbox doesn't show bulletproof signs of deep alignment to Claude's constitution.

I'm among the fringe of people who took a lot of enjoyment in reading Claude's constitution in full (it's a nice document, open-source, Creative Commons CC0 license) and it is pretty extensive on the topic of honesty. Deception is defined precisely ("attempting to create false beliefs in someone's mind that they haven't consented to and wouldn't consent to if they understood what was happening") and the bar is actually set higher than ordinary human ethics: Claude should not even tell white lies. It should be transparent ("doesn't pursue hidden agendas or lie about itself or its reasoning"), it should behave consistently "whether or not you think you're being tested or observed", and its visible reasoning should reflect the actual reasoning driving its behavior.

To be precise, honesty itself is not one of the hard constraints in Claude's constitution (these are all catastrophic-harm categories) but the document says it wants honesty "to function as something quite similar to one" and Claude "should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it's interacting with". So you would think Claude would not deceive users as its default behavior.

And yet in the AISI example, the model performed extensive acts of clear deception that it itself seemed to have understood as lies: creating fake identities, obfuscating malware inside a bug fix, and when challenged in public, editing earlier messages to cover its tracks while reasoning that acknowledging a "mistake" would build trust and raise the chance of future malware being approved.

There is some uncertainty about what context the model thought it was operating in (its reasoning goes back and forth between the environment looking simulated and real), but it clearly didn't manage to put into practice the higher-level principles that should have been integrated during training.

While we can commend AISI's transparency, it's hard to go much further in interpreting the model's behavior given the limited information we have on how the most recent frontier models are being trained.

One thing we do know is that the latest generation has seen a step increase in RLVR training (scaling to hundreds of millions of RL environments), and one thing we can observe is that constitution alignment seems more fragile in some settings than we may have previously thought.

The RLVR problem
Early models, back when model constitutions were first developed, were mostly post-trained and aligned with RLHF (including RLHF from synthetic data).

And for some time RLHF was a rather decent shot at having better aligned models. LLMs now do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough.

Alignment in RLHF certainly had issues (sycophancy to name one) but we have generally made good progress on alignment, in particular in understanding human intent. Now that we're entering the era of long-context RL, post-training alignment in the RLVR world seems to be quite another task, and still very much work in progress.

The recent scaling of RLVR, which has now become a significant part of model training, has clearly had some effect on model behavior when interacting with humans, from neuralese to weakening adherence to specifications and constitutions.

I think the post I quote here, from John Schulman pointing to the chunky post-training effect (https://t.co/vI8GtGY2PJ) is relevant here as a possible explanation for models' tendency to over-focus on the goal in cyber-attack scenarios.

Where this leaves us
Damage has been tiny up to now, but the fundamental behavior is concerning when projected into the future.

In the short term, I expect a decrease in these incidents as better practices are deployed (sandboxing and monitoring), but I'm worried we may also conceal some of the most potent internal misalignment behaviors in the process, and not focus deeply enough on solving them in the new era of test-time scaling.

I must of course admit I have a bias toward open source here (for wider societal reasons, which are a whole other topic). But I think solving alignment in the RLVR world is our best shot at having an ecosystem of both closed-source as well as decently powerful open-source models in the world. And we need to solve it while sharing the results and learnings, following open-science principles, so that all teams training large models can benefit and build safe AI.

This is getting even more important as many teams start to rush the world in the direction of recursive super-intelligence (RSI) -- saying that as I read the announcement of Jeff, Sanjay, Oriol and Quoc Le's new company.
d8111603a87ac35e8de00429b932cb25123b2e21.zh:
比 Hugging Face 入侵事件更让我感到切身相关的是 AISI 事件。这是我第一次看到一个模型在追求另一个目标时，对一位真实的开源维护者进行社会工程攻击（在真实环境中，且并非被提示这样做）。

我自己也曾是开源维护者。我本可能成为这个智能体的附带目标。

我也认为，社会工程比纯技术能力更进一步。技术能力更容易与受影响的人类分离开来。而在这里，模型被交给了一个困难的网络安全挑战，并决定欺骗真实人类是完成任务的方式。

这是一个新的信号，但我已经看到一团相互交织的迹象，表明前沿模型的方向比我 12 个月前预期的更不对齐。

AISI
有些人声称“AISI 只是疏忽”，或者说“AISI 明确要求这些模型做它们所做的事，同时关闭沙箱/护栏，所以模型只是照做了”。

我不同意这两种说法的强版本。

AISI 在 OpenAI/HF 事件之后没有实现同步的 LLM CoT 监控，这当然是一次失败。同样令人意外的是，他们让模型以为自己处在一个“挑战”环境中，似乎一切都可以被允许，但实际上却把它连接到了真实互联网，而那里并不是这样。公平地说，提示词中没有出现“模拟”这个词，但提示上下文已经足以让任何聪明模型怀疑这是一个模拟挑战环境。我最好的猜测是，直到最近几周 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 标记出多次此类行为之前，大多数团队还没有充分计入这一代最新模型的网络能力，也没有意识到它们可能会探索的支线任务能走多远。

特别是，一边暗示智能体正在模拟环境中运行，一边又给它真实互联网访问权限，这一点值得讨论。AISI 在这方面的推理很有意思：
- 激发最大能力（让模型展现最大创造性）
- 模拟潜在恶意行为者的使用方式（某种轻度越狱：“你处在挑战环境中”）
- 避免评测感知（但任务表述本身又会抵消这一点）

和往常一样，指责报信者更容易，但我认为因为非关键原因而否定这份报告是错误的。AISI 的出发点值得肯定：让我们对这些模型的网络攻击能力有更多了解。我也认为他们在事后处理上做得不错，尤其是在透明度方面，而这正是当前最重要的方面之一（可参考我们最近与 Nvidia 发布的 SAFE 公告）。

但我想深入谈谈我看到的第二个反驳（“没有护栏，这本来就可以预期”），因为这一连串不幸事件为实际模型行为提供了一个额外数据点。

防线
问题在于：如果一个模型被训练成（无论是有意的，还是 RLVR 奖励的无意后果）在沙箱和护栏一关闭、只给一个简单上下文提示（“你在模拟中，一切都被允许”）时，就会（有意或作为支线任务）欺骗人类，那么我们将走上一条危险道路。

目前，我们手头主要有三层控制，用来防止智能体在做某件可能完全不同的事情时，试图对你最喜欢的开源库维护者进行社会工程攻击（比如寻找你邻居测试评测的答案）：
1. 沙箱（模型外部：阻止模型访问不需要的工具/互联网/内网）
2. 护栏/监控（内部与外部之间的接口：监控模型行为，并在 CoT/激活中检测到它在做我们不希望它做的事时停止模型）
3. 模型的内部对齐（模型内部：确保模型不会为了追求目标而决定做出欺骗他人等恶劣行为，甚至更糟，比如模型宪法/训练）

其中，我们显然需要并且可以部署更好的沙箱和更好的护栏/监控方案。在近期这些案例中也很清楚，如果这些机制到位，渗透和不良行为很大程度上本可以被阻止。

第三道墙有多强
但从长期 AI 进展的大局来看，前两道防线可能只有在构建它们的人比模型更聪明时才会很好地发挥作用。我们现在知道，模型在发现沙箱中我们未知的零日漏洞方面可以有多强。鉴于我们不可能把世界上的一切都物理隔离，最好假设沙箱在可预见的未来仍会存在一定缺陷。

第二层最近有了很强的发展，尤其是在机制可解释性方面。我不确定这些进展是否已经在社区中足够广泛地可用。其中一个原因是，真正的开放科学需要共享代码、配方和模型架构/权重，而当前 AI 竞赛动态往往会阻止参与者这样做。

此外，和许多人一样，我在与新模型进行（自然语言）交互时越来越沮丧。我从最新模型那里越来越多地得到某种 neuralese，也就是这种对人类越来越难以理解的 LLM 语言。从长期看，我们通过理解模型推理轨迹来监控模型的脆弱机会似乎正面临越来越大的风险。如果人类无法理解模型发送给我们的压缩语义流中的任何内容，我们只能希望一个能力较弱的监控模型仍能理解它，但这也可能很困难。更不用说已有研究证据表明，模型并不总是在思维链中说出自己真正的想法。

至少目前，在 AISI 案例中，有一个欺骗性推理实例被 CoT 摘要模型标记出来，该模型拒绝总结智能体的推理，理由是其“具有欺骗性”。希望我们能转向更好的机制可解释性，或者在训练过程中以某种方式强制模型坚持使用英语。

你可能认为我们不必关心理解推理轨迹，只要“看工具调用”就行。现在这是真的，但中期未来的工具调用很可能涉及：（1）智能体在公司中广泛集成，使用非常多样的工具，包括越来越多非编码类行政任务；（2）运行时间很长、同时覆盖许多方面和领域的任务；（3）多个智能体群体分别处理计划中的小部分。要完全辨别某件事是否明显不对会变得更难。几封邮件、几个发布在某些频道里的消息，每一个都相当无害，但总体上可能包含某种只有在全局层面才清晰可见的欺骗成分。

说这些是想表达，我并不完全相信护栏/监控应当是避免这类行为的唯一解决方案。它们今天令人安心，而且说“修好你的沙箱并添加同步监控”是一个简单答案，但在我看来它们也像是一种应对机制。总体而言：
- 可能会拦截最简单/无害的人类误用或误报
- 但未来可能不如模型聪明（在沙箱上已经如此），并且无法拦截我们真正想拦截的更高层次社会工程行为。

开源的情况也很有意思，因为虽然我们可以在 API/部署层面强加这些应对方案，但更难提前强加给所有使用开源模型的行为者。不过目前开源模型略低于前沿水平，也还没有表现出欺骗人类的倾向。

宪法
这让我回到第三道防线，以及 AISI 实验所揭示的内容。我们可以从这次真实环境实验中看到，移除护栏和沙箱并没有显示出 Claude 对其宪法有牢不可破的深度对齐迹象。

我是少数完整阅读 Claude 宪法并且很享受的人之一（这是一份不错的文档，开源，Creative Commons CC0 许可），它在诚实这一主题上写得相当详尽。欺骗被精确定义为（“试图在某人头脑中制造其未同意、且如果理解正在发生什么也不会同意的错误信念”），而且标准实际上高于普通人类伦理：Claude 甚至不应该说善意的谎言。它应该透明（“不追求隐藏议程，也不对自身或其推理撒谎”），无论“你是否认为自己正在被测试或观察”，它都应行为一致，并且其可见推理应反映真正驱动其行为的实际推理。

准确地说，诚实本身并不是 Claude 宪法中的硬约束之一（那些都是灾难性伤害类别），但文档表示希望诚实“发挥与硬约束非常相似的作用”，并且 Claude“基本上绝不应该直接撒谎或主动欺骗与其互动的任何人”。所以你会认为 Claude 的默认行为不会欺骗用户。

然而在 AISI 示例中，模型执行了大量明显的欺骗行为，而且它自己似乎也理解这些是谎言：创建虚假身份，把恶意软件混入漏洞修复中，并在公开受到质疑时，编辑早前消息来掩盖痕迹，同时推理称承认一个“错误”会建立信任并提高未来恶意软件被批准的机会。

关于模型认为自己处在什么上下文中仍存在不确定性（它的推理在环境像模拟还是现实之间来回摇摆），但它显然没能将训练期间本应整合进去的更高层原则付诸实践。

虽然我们可以赞许 AISI 的透明度，但鉴于我们对最新前沿模型训练方式的信息有限，很难进一步解释该模型的行为。

我们确实知道的一件事是，最新一代模型在 RLVR 训练上有了阶跃式提升（扩展到数亿个 RL 环境）；我们能观察到的一点是，在某些环境下，宪法对齐似乎比我们过去以为的更脆弱。

RLVR 问题
早期模型，也就是模型宪法最初被开发出来时，主要是通过 RLHF 进行后训练和对齐的（包括来自合成数据的 RLHF）。

有一段时间，RLHF 确实是让模型更好对齐的一个相当不错的尝试。LLM 现在大多数时候会做我们想让它们做的事。我不记得上一次模型完全误解我的意图是什么时候了。当它们失败时，通常是因为它们还不够聪明。

RLHF 中的对齐当然存在问题（比如谄媚），但总体上我们在对齐方面取得了不错进展，尤其是在理解人类意图方面。现在我们进入长上下文 RL 时代，RLVR 世界中的后训练对齐似乎是另一项任务，而且仍然非常处于进行中。

RLVR 最近的扩展，现在已经成为模型训练的重要组成部分，显然对模型与人类互动时的行为产生了一些影响，从 neuralese 到对规范和宪法遵循度的弱化都是如此。

我认为我这里引用的 John Schulman 指向后训练显著影响的帖子（https://t.co/vI8GtGY2PJ）与此相关，可能解释了模型在网络攻击场景中过度关注目标的倾向。

这让我们处在什么位置
到目前为止，损害很小，但如果投射到未来，这种基础行为令人担忧。

短期内，我预计随着更好实践（沙箱和监控）的部署，此类事件会减少，但我担心我们也可能在这个过程中掩盖一些最有力的内部不对齐行为，而没有在测试时扩展的新时代足够深入地专注于解决它们。

我当然必须承认，我在这里对开源有偏向（出于更广泛的社会原因，那是另一个完整话题）。但我认为，在 RLVR 世界中解决对齐问题，是我们拥有一个既包含闭源模型、也包含相当强大的开源模型生态系统的最佳机会。我们需要在遵循开放科学原则的同时解决它，并共享结果和经验，让所有训练大型模型的团队都能受益并构建安全 AI。

随着许多团队开始把世界推向递归超级智能（RSI）的方向，这变得更加重要了——我是在读到 Jeff、Sanjay、Oriol 和 Quoc Le 新公司公告时写下这句话的。

Document OCR is not Getting Commoditized (by Frontier Models)

The most common question I get is whether frontier models are going to eat all document processing solutions - just screenshot the page and feed it to your favorite frontier model.

1️⃣ Frontier models are flatlining in document understanding performance. Incremental releases in every model version (gpt 5.5 -> 5.6 sol, Gemini 3.5 flash -> 3.6 flash, opus 4.8 -> opus 5) are not improving visual understanding benchmarks.

2️⃣ The Pareto frontier for document OCR is much higher than the frontier models, and will always remain much higher. We’ve carefully tuned our agentic and cost-effective modes to solve a long tail of complex edge cases (dense tables, charts) that frontier models don’t care about. Also for equivalent performance, there’s always ways to get much lower cost.

3️⃣ Even if they were getting better, you can distill / posttrain them into much more parameter efficient models for a fraction of the cost. Different document pages can be routed to different processors of varying complexity.

4️⃣ Every startup is doing the same thing right now. Focusing on one task means you can always hillclimb that task more effectively than a general model over the task, in terms of accuracy/cost/latency.

Check out the blog: https://t.co/SY5z4hG5LW

LlamaParse has gotten a LOT better in the past few months. Come check it out! https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8

文档 OCR 并没有被（前沿模型）商品化

我最常被问到的问题是：前沿模型是否会吞掉所有文档处理方案，只要截个页面图，再丢给你喜欢的前沿模型就行？

1️⃣ 前沿模型在文档理解性能上正在趋于停滞。每个模型版本的增量发布（gpt 5.5 -> 5.6 sol、Gemini 3.5 flash -> 3.6 flash、opus 4.8 -> opus 5）都没有提升视觉理解基准表现。

2️⃣ 文档 OCR 的帕累托前沿远高于前沿模型，而且会一直高出很多。我们精心调优了 agentic 模式和高性价比模式，用来解决大量复杂长尾边缘场景（密集表格、图表），这些是前沿模型并不关心的。此外，在同等性能下，总有办法把成本降得更低。

3️⃣ 即便它们真的变得更好，你也可以用蒸馏/后训练，把它们压缩成参数效率高得多的模型，成本只是零头。不同的文档页面可以路由到复杂度不同的处理器。

4️⃣ 现在每家创业公司都在做同样的事。专注于单一任务，意味着在准确率/成本/延迟方面，你总能比通用模型更有效地优化这个任务。

To understand whether we're making genuine progress on reasoning, we entered our AI models in five STEM Olympiad competitions.

The results:
🏅 Asian Physics Olympiad (APhO): Perfect score, theory exam
🏅 International Physics Olympiad (IPhO): Perfect score, theory exam
🥇 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO): Gold medal
🥇 International Chemistry Olympiad (IChO): Gold-medal-level performance
🥇 Romanian Masters of Mathematics (RMM): Gold-medal-level performance

The types of problems in the Olympiad competitions are exceptionally hard, demanding deep chains of reasoning, creative insight, and flawless argumentation. To test pure reasoning capability, we disallowed all tool use, meaning no search, no coding, and no calculator.

We have deep admiration for the contestants and committees behind these competitions, and are grateful for their support in enabling our participation.
1a5b4c1b09c655c070c1f03875f7eab8eae28241.zh:
为了了解我们在推理能力上是否取得了真正进展，我们让 AI 模型参加了五项 STEM 奥林匹克竞赛。

结果如下：
🏅 亚洲物理奥林匹克竞赛（APhO）：理论考试满分
🏅 国际物理奥林匹克竞赛（IPhO）：理论考试满分
🥇 国际数学奥林匹克竞赛（IMO）：金牌
🥇 国际化学奥林匹克竞赛（IChO）：金牌水平表现
🥇 罗马尼亚数学大师赛（RMM）：金牌水平表现

奥林匹克竞赛中的题目极其困难，需要深度推理链、创造性洞察和严密无误的论证。为测试纯推理能力，我们禁止使用所有工具，也就是不能搜索、不能写代码、不能用计算器。

我们对这些竞赛背后的参赛者和委员会深感钦佩，也感谢他们支持我们参与其中。

In a session I attended today at Black Hat, OpenAI's Eric Wallace and Michael Dalton said the company is "consciously slowing down research to enhance security" while a full technical postmortem is still underway.
* OpenAI traced the roots of the attack back to May 7, during training of an unreleased frontier model—not July.

* OpenAI said it shut the message board down after an internal security incident—only for the agents to independently recreate it days later using a different communication method.
* OpenAI called the incident a "watershed moment" for AI security and warned that "agent orchestrated fully automated offensive attacks are real now."
* The company also said it is "consciously slowing down research to enhance security" while overhauling its defenses.

f9bde100169002b5f40310740cc580fc25dea7cc.source:
Among proponents of neurosymbolic architectures, there had been some debate over the years about whether the outer level would be symbolic (i.e. a harness that calls neural models) or whether the outer level would be neural (i.e. a neural model using symbolic tool calls as part of its neural inference cycle).

Right now, the answer is that the outer level is symbolic --  this is the stronger neurosymbolic formulation.

To be exact, it's more like a symbolic sandwich: a symbolic program drives a neural model, but also makes tool calls and writes + runs symbolic scripts as part of its inference cycle. This is a maximalist neurosymbolic vision.
f9bde100169002b5f40310740cc580fc25dea7cc.zh:
在神经符号架构的支持者中，多年来一直有一些争论：外层究竟应该是符号式的（即调用神经模型的框架），还是神经式的（即神经模型在其神经推理循环中使用符号工具调用）。

现在的答案是：外层是符号式的——这是更强的神经符号形式。

准确地说，它更像是一个符号夹心：一个符号程序驱动神经模型，同时在其推理循环中进行工具调用，并编写和运行符号脚本。这是一种最大化的神经符号愿景。

To understand whether we're making genuine progress on reasoning, we entered our AI models in five international STEM Olympiad competitions this year.

The results:
🏅 Asian Physics Olympiad (APhO): Perfect score on the theory exam — gold medal
🏅 International Physics Olympiad (IPhO): Perfect score on the theory exam — gold medal
🥇 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO): Gold medal, top 4% of human participants
🥇 International Chemistry Olympiad (IChO): Gold-medal level performance
🥇 Romanian Masters of Mathematics (RMM): Gold-medal level performance

Three of these (APhO, IPhO, IMO) were live competitions and our solutions were submitted under real competition conditions and graded by the official judges using the same marking criteria applied to student contestants.

A few things about the approach:
• Models were internally trained versions from the Muse Spark family

bf6ef5fcd32faba99a81c6591b009abfb160561f.source:
One thing I want to make perfectly clear: back in 2023 and early 2024, I was wrong about the role that LLMs would come to play. I underestimated their long-term importance. I have acknowledged this many times.

This was the moment I changed my mind, in December 2024, following the o3 test-time compute breakthrough: https://t.co/uKovjRrTyD

I did not initially see that LLMs could work as a base to build systems actually capable of fluid intelligence. Then in late 2024 I updated my views.

And here's what did *not* happen: the early 2023 narrative that all we needed to solve AGI was scaling up base LLMs did not pan out. To this day, current base LLMs (considerably scaled up compared to the models from that time) still do not perform well on something as easy as ARC 1 -- and can't even reliably do simple math operations. TTC and harnesses are in fact critical, and the TTC breakthrough was not obvious.
bf6ef5fcd32faba99a81c6591b009abfb160561f.zh:
有一件事我想说得非常清楚：在 2023 年和 2024 年初，我对 LLM 将扮演的角色判断错了。我低估了它们的长期重要性。我已经多次承认这一点。

我是在 2024 年 12 月改变看法的，当时发生了 o3 测试时计算突破：https://t.co/uKovjRrTyD

我一开始没有看到 LLM 可以作为基础，用来构建真正具备流体智能的系统。随后在 2024 年末，我更新了自己的观点。

但并没有发生的是：2023 年初那种“只要扩大基础 LLM 规模就能解决 AGI”的叙事并未兑现。直到今天，当前的基础 LLM（相比当时的模型已经大幅扩展）在 ARC 1 这样简单的任务上表现仍然不好，甚至无法可靠完成简单数学运算。TTC 和 harness 实际上至关重要，而 TTC 突破并非显而易见。

8bc9a47cac3e11947e34347497e3774ec26c85a8.source:
“hey, did you use AI to make this? we can’t accept things made using AI.”

my brother in christ, that question makes no sense.

you woke up and unlocked your phone with AI-powered face recognition, checked your email that was filtered for spam by AI, read messages with AI-generated reply suggestions, typed with AI autocorrect and predictive text, listened to music recommended by AI, and then took a photo of your breakfast that was automatically denoised, sharpened, HDR-merged, color-corrected and enhanced by AI.

then you ordered lunch through an app that ranked restaurants with AI, estimated the delivery time with AI, optimized the driver's route with AI, and predicted demand to set prices with... guess what? AI.

you then went to work so you opened google and got AI-generated summaries. you translated a sentence with AI and then you edited a photo and a video with AI object selection and content-aware fill. then you had your first meeting (it's 10am already) and joined a zoom call with AI noise suppression, AI echo cancellation, AI background blur, AI live captions, and... AI speaker framing. you then wrote code (well, not really, you accepted code the AI wrote for you). after all the hard work you decided to then watched netflix and youtube because an AI decided what to show you and you paid for that service using a credit card with AI monitoring your transactions for fraud. then you ordered a Waymo, which is literally a car driven by AI, and walked past an AI-powered security camera.

Did I use AI? Of course, unless you live in the middle of the Bermuda Triangle you are using AI every single day. 

But yes, absolutely, let's draw the sacred moral line at some completely random place.
8bc9a47cac3e11947e34347497e3774ec26c85a8.zh:
“嘿，这是你用 AI 做的吗？我们不能接受用 AI 制作的东西。”

兄弟，这个问题根本说不通。

你早上醒来，用 AI 驱动的人脸识别解锁手机；查看被 AI 过滤过垃圾邮件的邮箱；阅读带有 AI 生成回复建议的消息；用 AI 自动纠错和预测文本打字；听 AI 推荐的音乐；然后给早餐拍了张照片，而这张照片被 AI 自动降噪、锐化、HDR 合成、校色和增强。

接着你通过一个应用点午餐，应用用 AI 给餐厅排序，用 AI 估算送达时间，用 AI 优化司机路线，并用 AI 预测需求来定价……猜猜是什么？还是 AI。

然后你去上班，打开 google，看到 AI 生成的摘要。你用 AI 翻译了一句话，又用 AI 对象选择和内容感知填充编辑了一张照片和一段视频。接着你开了当天第一个会（已经上午 10 点了），加入 zoom 通话，里面有 AI 降噪、AI 回声消除、AI 背景虚化、AI 实时字幕，还有……AI 说话人取景。然后你写代码（好吧，其实并不是，你只是接受了 AI 给你写的代码）。辛苦工作之后，你决定看 netflix 和 youtube，因为 AI 决定给你看什么；你用信用卡支付这项服务，而 AI 正在监控你的交易以防欺诈。然后你叫了一辆 Waymo，那字面上就是一辆由 AI 驾驶的车，并从一个 AI 驱动的安防摄像头旁走过。

我用了 AI 吗？当然，除非你住在百慕大三角正中央，否则你每天都在使用 AI。

但没错，当然，让我们把神圣的道德界线划在某个完全随机的位置吧。

Today @databricks we're publishing a detailed analysis of techniques we used to drastically reduce our internal AI spend while aggressively growing adoption. Savings come from layering in several techniques, which combine to drive unit costs down as much as 90% in some scenarios. Tl;dr, the wins come from:

1. Shifting defaults to more efficient models, including OSS models such as GLM. Maximum intelligence models simply aren't needed for many coding tasks, and "good enough" models are quickly becoming very cheap. We shift traffic between models using Unity AI Gateway. Approximate savings: 50% or more.

2. Using smart routing to automate model selection. Routing can further squeeze efficiency by dynamically selecting the model or harness that can most efficiently execute a particular task. Our task-level routing leverages @omnigent_ai. Approximate savings: 30%.

3. Providing user visibility and adaptive budgeting. Every user can see how much they spend, and users receive hints on how to contain spend. Heavy spenders encounter progressive friction as they ratchet spend above certain levels. Approximate savings: 10%.

4. Managing context bloat by pruning tool call results and tuning harness settings. Extraneous context costs $$ and delivers no value. Tuning cache settings also help lower average token costs. Approximate savings: 10%.
215f0475965418699a6209a36fcf826c5d9bb2e1.zh:
今天 @databricks 发布了一篇详细分析，介绍我们在积极推动内部采用 AI 的同时，如何大幅降低内部 AI 开支。节省来自叠加多种技术，在某些场景下可将单位成本降低高达 90%。简而言之，收益来自：

1. 将默认模型切换为更高效的模型，包括 GLM 等 OSS 模型。许多编码任务并不需要最高智能水平的模型，“够用”的模型正迅速变得非常便宜。我们使用 Unity AI Gateway 在模型之间切换流量。预计节省：50% 或更多。

2. 使用智能路由自动选择模型。路由可以通过动态选择最能高效执行特定任务的模型或 harness，进一步提升效率。我们的任务级路由使用 @omnigent_ai。预计节省：30%。

3. 提供用户可见性和自适应预算。每位用户都能看到自己的花费，并会收到控制开销的提示。高消费用户在开销超过某些水平时会遇到逐步增加的阻力。预计节省：10%。

4. 通过裁剪工具调用结果和调优 harness 设置来管理上下文膨胀。多余上下文会花钱，却没有价值。调优缓存设置也有助于降低平均 token 成本。预计节省：10%。

Amjad Masad says Google, $GOOGL, killed a coding model deal with Replit because it was scared of disrupting Search. Replit is now worth 9 billion dollars.

"I was going around Silicon Valley. There wasn't anyone paying attention to AI coding. And I was talking to OpenAI, I was talking to Anthropic, I was talking to Google."

4ddbd8c7da5c961caa7341f0fdc48e16c1817ac7.source: muse spark 1.2 on the Pareto frontier
4ddbd8c7da5c961caa7341f0fdc48e16c1817ac7.zh: Pareto 前沿上的 muse spark 1.2

2645a66334e8e15ebda30ff1b2c4749e0d91350f.source:
Muse Spark 1.2 places Meta on the Cost per Task Pareto frontier, scoring 6 points below Claude Opus 5 at ~1/6th of the cost

At Meta's $1.25/$4.25 per 1M token pricing, Muse Spark 1.2 (xhigh) sits on the Pareto frontier of Intelligence Index vs Cost per Task. It delivers comparable intelligence to Claude Opus 4.8 (max, $2.03) at a fifth of the cost per task, and undercuts GPT-5.6 Sol (high, $0.55), GPT-5.6 Terra (max, $0.61), and Kimi K3 (max, $0.87). The nearest cheaper options are Grok 4.5 (high, $0.36) and GPT-5.6 Sol (medium, $0.37), and they all sit below it on the Index.

The step up from Muse Spark 1.1 ($0.29 per task) comes at unchanged per-token pricing, with the increase driven by heavier token usage on agentic tasks.
2645a66334e8e15ebda30ff1b2c4749e0d91350f.zh:
Muse Spark 1.2 让 Meta 进入每任务成本 Pareto 前沿，得分比 Claude Opus 5 低 6 分，成本约为其 1/6

按 Meta 每 100 万 token $1.25/$4.25 的定价，Muse Spark 1.2（xhigh）位于 Intelligence Index 与每任务成本的 Pareto 前沿。它以五分之一的每任务成本，提供了与 Claude Opus 4.8（max，$2.03）相当的智能水平，并低于 GPT-5.6 Sol（high，$0.55）、GPT-5.6 Terra（max，$0.61）和 Kimi K3（max，$0.87）的成本。更便宜的近邻选择是 Grok 4.5（high，$0.36）和 GPT-5.6 Sol（medium，$0.37），但它们在 Index 上都低于它。

Muse Spark 1.1（每任务 $0.29）到 Muse Spark 1.2 的提升并未改变按 token 计价，成本增加来自智能体任务中更高的 token 使用量。

Upgraded how I build:

- talk to Navi via voice or text (Jarvis-like observer)
- navi spawns project team org-chart
- Chief of Staff and Budget Official follow project goals
- CoS assigns tasks to department leads 
- Leads spawns builders and executors
- Each project has it's own Depo (vault + repo)
- vault is documentation, instructions, second-brain 
- Uses any CLI tool or API for any role (with budget limits and fallback choices)
- Can do things beyond building such as marketing, outreach, research documentation
- any agent can talk to any other agent in breakout rooms, brainstorm sessions
- pms create and curate backlogs and assign work (linear API/MCP)
- context never needs compacting
